title: Cap. 7 Scholastici: Scotus and Hugh of St Victor on elect-directed passion
pass_a_gloss: 4. Scotus on the Sentences, book 3, distinction 19, the single question, has many things which greatly help to illustrate our opinion, this first of all: Just as the Word foresaw his passion to be offered to the Father for the elect, so he efficaciously offered it unto effect, and the whole Trinity efficaciously accepted the passion for them, and for no others was it efficaciously offered, nor accepted from eternity. Scotus acknowledges that from the eternal decree of the whole Trinity Christ's passion was offered and accepted for the elect in a certain singular manner and with a special intention. 5. Hugh of Saint Victor, On the Sacraments of the Faith, book 1, part 8, chapter 7. Where he institutes a treatment On the passion of Christ, he writes thus: Human nature was corrupted through sin, and the whole was due to damnation through sin, and therefore, if the whole had been damned, it would not have been injustice. But grace came, and chose some from the mass of the universe through mercy unto salvation, but deserted some through justice unto damnation. Hugh openly teaches that Christ coming into the world, and offering himself for the sins of the human race, had a singular respect toward the elect, whom he chose from the mass of the universe, and whom he decreed to lead unto salvation by the merits of his death according to God's eternal good pleasure, and in fact always leads.
pass_b_english: 4. Scotus (Sentences III, dist. 19, single q.) has much that illustrates our view. First: just as the Word foresaw his passion to be offered to the Father for the elect, so he offered it effectually unto its effect, and the whole Trinity effectually accepted that passion for them; for no others was it effectually offered or eternally accepted. So Scotus grants that by the Trinity's eternal decree Christ's passion was offered and accepted for the elect in a singular way, with special intention. 5. Hugh of St Victor (On the Sacraments I.8.7), treating Christ's passion: Human nature was corrupted by sin and wholly owed to damnation; if all had been damned, that would not have been injustice. But grace came and chose some from the mass of the whole by mercy unto salvation, and left some by justice unto damnation. Hugh teaches plainly that Christ, coming and offering himself for the race's sins, kept a singular eye on the elect he chose from that mass, whom he decreed — and in fact always does — to bring to salvation by his death's merits according to God's eternal good pleasure.
source_text: 4. Scotus in 3. Sentent. dist. 19. quest. unica, multa habet quae valde conducunt ad sententiam nostram illustrandam, illud inprimis, Sicut Verbum praevidit passionem suam Patri offerendam pro electis, sic eam efficaciter obtulit in effectum, & tota Trinitas pro eis passionem efficaciter acceptavit, & pro nullis aliis fuit efficaciter oblata, nec ab aeterno acceptata. Agnoscit Scotus, ex aeterno decreto totius Trinitatis passionem Christi fuisse singulari quodam modo & speciali intentione oblatam & acceptatam pro electis. 5. Hugo de S. Victore, De Sacr. fid. lib. 1. part. 8. cap. 7. Ubi tractationem instituit De passione Christi, sic scribit, Natura humana per peccatum corrupta fuit, & tota per peccatum damnationi debita erat, & idcirco, si tota damnata fuisset, injustitia non fuisset. Venit autem gratia, & elegit quosdam de massa universitatis per misericordiam ad salutem, quosdam autem per justitiam deseruit ad damnationem. Aperte docet Hugo, Christum in mundum venientem, & pro peccatis humani generis sese offerentem, habuisse respectum singularem ad electos, quos de massa universitatis elegit, quosque ad salutem pro aeterno Dei beneplacito per merita mortis suae perducere decrevit, & de facto semper perducit.
